cur: Each user tells Mondai how many hours they can give each week, the first time they open the Action Hub. Everything else is planned from that number.
new: Each user tells Mondai how many hours they can give each week, the first time they open the Action Hub. Everything else is planned from that number. Mondai asks instead of learning the number from how the user works, because learning it would leave the first two or three weeks without a real plan. The risk is that users promise more time than they have, so the screen has them type an exact number of hours, which makes them count, instead of picking a generous range. If their weeks keep falling short, the plan can lower it later.
tactic: Refute the rejected option (cs-t24); name what it cost (cs-t21); Chekhov's rifle (cs-t18)
why: This is the input the whole framework hangs on, and the page never says why the user declares it instead of Mondai learning it, the first thing a hiring manager would ask. The archive has the rejected option with its reason (learning it means two or three weeks with no real plan) and the cost of the choice (users overestimate their time), with the fix for each. Naming the cost is what makes the choice read as judgment; the bank says a decision with no cost reads as an observation. It also plants a rifle that fires later: the plan can lower it later is paid off by Recalibration in Start of week, named there and not here, so nothing leans on a concept the reader has not met. Written as how Mondai works, not as I decided, because the archive holds this reasoning and your record does not show it as your argument. Longer than the label slot now; if it does not fit, the last sentence is the one to keep. Reader check round 3 flagged the so in the risk sentence 3 of 3 (why would typing a number help?), so the sentence now says how: typing makes them count.
src: Archive:70 (PARAPHRASE, archive premise): observed capacity has a two to three week cold start; declared capacity builds a real plan on day one and is revised later through Recalibration; planning fallacy is a real risk, so the screen uses manual hour input rather than pre filled buckets. Recalibration only lowers capacity (round 2 review finding, CONFIRMED). Which makes them count is my reading of why manual input answers planning fallacy (ASSUMED; the archive gives the choice, not the mechanism).

cur: A week that comes up short can feel like failing, and that feeling makes users less likely to keep going. So nobody has to decide what to do with it while they’re already behind: an unfinished Action Item moves into the next week on its own. An earlier version asked users to choose at that moment, with the math on screen, and we cut it because it felt like a gate, not a guide. A week can only hold the hours the user set aside for it (their capacity). The Rollover takes up some of the next week’s capacity, so some of that week’s Action Items move to the week after, and the ones behind them move along too. That is why the pace date moves later, and since the journey pace is the last Pathway’s pace, the journey moves with it. The target stays where it was.
